query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐temperature corrosive environments typical of chemical processing and nuclear power (e.g., liquid lead or lead–bismuth eutectic), steels that incorporate small amounts of strong oxide‐forming elements (such as Al and/or Si) and that develop a refined grain boundary (or oxide dispersion strengthened) structure resist corrosion because these features synergistically promote the rapid nucleation and growth of a continuous, dense, dual‐layer oxide film (principally Al2O3 and Cr2O3) at grain boundaries. This protective film retards further oxygen and metal ion diffusion and thus slows dissolution of the underlying matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional ferritic/martensitic steel (e.g., T91 or 9Cr type), which in its baseline state forms only a partially protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Introduce minor alloying additions of Al and/or Si and/or use processing methods to refine the grain (or dispersion-strengthen the matrix) to enhance grain-boundary area and ordering.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature, dissolving/liquid metal environments (e.g., liquid Pb/LBE at temperatures above 550 °C) with controlled oxygen content that is near the threshold for protective oxide growth, as well as conditions relevant to aggressive chemical processing fluids.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a graded, well-adherent dual oxide layer (dense inner Al2O3 combined with a supportive Cr2O3 outer or intermediate layer) that nucleates preferentially at the refined grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Alloying with Al/Si increases local oxygen affinity at grain boundaries in a refined (or ODS) microstructure, accelerating the in situ formation of a continuous, low-porosity oxide film. This barrier limits the ingress of oxygen and the outward diffusion of metal ions, thereby slowing the dissolution (or lead-induced dissolution) of corrosion-prone elements. In effect, the grain boundary engineering synergizes with chemical composition adjustments to stabilize the passivation film against prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline steels without these modifications, the treated steels will develop thinner, more continuous and adherent oxide films, exhibit lower corrosion rates (as measured by reduced penetration depth and lower electrochemical dissolution currents), and display improved passivation behavior under identical high-temperature liquid metal or chemically aggressive conditions.
generation.baseline: Standard T91 or 9Cr steels processed without additional Al/Si or grain refinement, which under similar conditions form less protective, discontinuous oxide layers and show higher corrosion/dissolution rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for steels operating in environments where temperature, oxygen concentration, and corrosive species (e.g., liquid Pb or LBE, aggressive chemicals) challenge the stability of passive films—typically above 550 °C in controlled oxidative conditions. Outside these conditions (e.g., in ambient temperature aqueous media without aggressive dissolution), the dominant corrosion mechanisms may differ.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on findings that (1) adding Al (and high oxygen-affinity elements) promotes formation of protective Al2O3 films in steels (PMC10054900::web::003::1_introduction and PMC10054900::web::023::4_conclusions) and (2) Si additions improve oxide film stability in T91 steel in LBE (PMC9028533::web::000::abstract and PMC9028533::web::023::4_discussion). The new element of the proposal is the explicit role of a refined (or ODS) grain structure to mediate the rapid diffusion and nucleation of the protective film. Uncertainty remains regarding the relative contributions of grain boundary density versus bulk alloy composition, especially considering conflicting observations that fine grains can sometimes accelerate dissolution if the oxide film is incomplete (PMC10054900::web::015::3_3_2_9cr_ods).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one set using the standard T91 or 9Cr composition with conventional grain size, and a second set with identical base chemistry but modified by adding minor amounts of Al/Si and processed to achieve a refined (or oxide dispersion strengthened) grain structure. Expose both sets to a controlled liquid-metal (Pb or LBE) environment at temperatures above 550 °C with controlled oxygen content for a prolonged period (e.g., 1000–2000 h).
measurements: Determine oxide film thickness, continuity, and composition using SEM/EDS and XPS.
Measure corrosion/dissolution rates via weight loss and electrochemical methods (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization).
Assess microstructural evolution by TEM or EBSD to confirm grain boundary refinement and oxide dispersion.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the modified steels do not display a statistically significant improvement in oxide film quality and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or greater corrosion depths, non-continuous oxide layers, and comparable or higher electrochemical dissolution rates) compared to the baseline steels under identical test conditions.

If introducing very fine oxide particles with a high number density into the matrix of steel, the operation temperature can be increased to 700 °C []. AbstractThe 9–12% Cr ferritic–martensitic heat-resistant steel is the main candidate structural material for the Lead-cooled Faster Reactor. The lower Gibbs free energy change of Si oxide can promote the formation of a stable oxide layer, which can improve the corrosion resistance of the material. Therefore, it is of great significance to study the effect of silicon (Si) on the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE). The corrosion resistance of T91 steel with Si contents of 0.5 wt.%, 1.3 wt.%, and 2.0 wt.%, both in dynamic and static LBE at 550 °C, was investigated. The microstructure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM), while the oxide films were characterized by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Results show that the addition of Si is conducive to improving the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in LBE. T91 steel with high Si content has a thinner and more stable oxide film. The change of Si content can change the contact angle between the steel and LBE, and the contact angle is the largest when the Si content is 1.3 wt.%. The corrosion failure modes of materials in LBE are oxidation and dissolution, and the root cause is diffusion. On the one hand, the matrix material diffuses into LBE, on the other hand, oxygen diffuses into the matrix. The corrosion mechanism and oxide film behavior of 9–12% Cr steel in LBR were studied, and a more classical oxide film growth model was put forward []. In this study, the change of oxide film after the addition of Si is studied, the formation sequence of oxide film in different layers is analyzed from the perspective of the formation energy of various oxides, and a new model is proposed. Excessively high oxygen content in LBE will produce a thick oxide film which can protect the material from further corrosion, but the falling off of the oxide film is easy to block the flow channel, thus affecting the reactor operation. It is hard to form a continuous oxide film in the oxygen-depleted LBE solution, so that the matrix cannot be protected from corrosion. Therefore, the ideal oxygen content in the alloy is of great significance for improving the corrosion resistance of structural materials in LBE.
